questions.stem: About 2% of extracted invoice records are rejected by the ERP because of malformed JSON: missing brackets, trailing commas and unescaped quotes in supplier names. The prompt currently says "Return JSON matching this structure" followed by an example. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Extend the example with tricky cases (quotes and commas in names) and add an explicit instruction to escape special characters.
options.why: This lowers the error rate, but it is still probabilistic.

options.text: Use an extraction tool whose `input_schema` is the invoice schema, and require it via `tool_choice`.
options.why: Tool use with a JSON schema removes syntax errors.

options.text: Run the output through a JSON-repair library before sending it to the ERP, and log any record the library can't repair.
options.why: Repairs can silently change values, and some records will still fail.

options.text: Set the temperature to 0, so the model produces the same well-formed structure it shows on most documents.
options.why: Lower temperature doesn't guarantee well-formed output.

questions.explanation: `tool_use` with an input schema is the most reliable way to get syntactically valid structured output.

questions.stem: After switching to schema-enforced tool use, JSON syntax errors have disappeared. But some records still put the invoice date in `due_date`, or record a tax amount as the line total. A product manager asks why the schema didn't prevent this. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: The schema isn't in strict mode. Enabling strict mode makes the model validate field meanings as well as types.
options.why: Strict mode enforces the schema's structure, not the meaning of values.

options.text: The model occasionally ignores schemas under load, so the pipeline should validate the structure again on receipt.
options.why: The structure is being respected. The values are wrong.

options.text: Schemas guarantee structure and types, not meaning. Add semantic validation (due ≥ issue date, totals reconcile) and clearer guidance.
options.why: Schemas eliminate syntax errors, not semantic ones.

options.text: Both fields share the `date` format, so the model can't tell them apart. Renaming them `date_1` and `date_2` fixes it.
options.why: Less descriptive names make the confusion worse, not better.

questions.explanation: Schemas give you syntax and shape. Semantic errors need validation, retry and better prompting.

questions.stem: Many bills of lading have no container number, because the goods ship as loose cargo. The schema marks `container_number` as a required string. Auditors found plausible-looking but invented container numbers in 6% of records. What is the best schema change?

options.text: Make `container_number` nullable or optional, and instruct the model to return `null` when it is absent.
options.why: A required field with no source data pushes the model to fabricate a value.

options.text: Keep the field required, and add a regex pattern for the ISO 6346 container format to reject invented values.
options.why: Invented values can match the format. The pressure to fabricate is still there.

options.text: Keep the field required, with a default of `"UNKNOWN"` that the model uses when no container number is present.
options.why: A magic string pollutes downstream data. `null` is the honest representation.

options.text: Remove `container_number` from the schema and extract it in a separate optional pass only for containerised shipments.
options.why: This adds a pass and complexity when a nullable field solves the problem directly.

questions.explanation: Make fields nullable or optional when the source may lack them, so the model isn't pushed to fabricate values.

questions.stem: `document_type` is an enum of `invoice`, `bill_of_lading` and `customs_form`. Suppliers have started sending packing lists and credit notes, which are being forced into the wrong categories and then routed to the wrong ERP queues. What is the best fix?

options.text: Replace the enum with a free-text field, so the model can describe new document types accurately as they appear.
options.why: This loses the consistency that downstream routing needs.

options.text: Instruct the model to choose the closest matching type when a document doesn't fit any category exactly.
options.why: This guarantees misclassification and wrong routing.

options.text: Add `packing_list` and `credit_note` to the enum now, and add new values whenever another type shows up in production.
options.why: This is reactive. Each new type will be misrouted until someone notices it.

options.text: Add `other` (with a `document_type_detail` string) and `unclear` to the enum, so unknown types have an honest option.
options.why: Escape-hatch enum values prevent forced misclassification.

questions.explanation: Enum design should include `other` plus a detail field, and `unclear`, for cases outside the known categories.

questions.stem: A validator finds that `line_items` don't sum to `subtotal` on 4% of invoices. A manual check shows that most cases are extraction mistakes, such as a missed line or a misread digit, rather than supplier errors. What is the most effective automated recovery?

options.text: Re-run extraction with the same prompt up to three times, and accept the first result that passes validation.
options.why: Blind retries without feedback often repeat the same mistake.

options.text: Retry with the document plus the specific validation error appended, such as "items sum to 1,240.00 but subtotal is 1,420.00".
options.why: Retries with specific error feedback let the model correct targeted mistakes.

options.text: Overwrite `subtotal` with the computed line-item sum, since extraction mistakes are the most common cause.
options.why: Genuine supplier errors would be hidden instead of flagged.

options.text: Route every mismatched invoice to human review immediately, since financial data shouldn't be corrected by automation.
options.why: Most of these are recoverable extraction errors, so this overloads reviewers.

questions.explanation: Validation-retry loops should feed back the specific error so that the model can fix it.

questions.stem: Some customs forms fail validation because the required HS tariff code is missing. Three retries, each with the specific error fed back, still fail. On inspection, the codes are not visible anywhere in those scans. What should happen next?

options.text: Raise the retry limit to ten with stronger wording, since the model may find the code in a less obvious part of the form.
options.why: This wastes cost and raises the risk that the model eventually fabricates a code.

options.text: Look up the supplier's most frequently used HS code in past records, and fill it in with a low-confidence flag.
options.why: This fabricates regulated data, even with a flag.

options.text: Stop retrying, because the data isn't in the source. Route the record to human review with the reason.
options.why: Retries can't recover information that isn't in the source.

options.text: Re-run extraction with a larger model and higher image resolution, to read fine print the current setup might miss.
options.why: The code isn't in the document, so a better reader won't find it.

questions.explanation: Retry loops have limits: when the source lacks the data, escalate instead of retrying.

questions.stem: Finance wants to catch invoices where the printed total doesn't match the line items, whether the cause is an extraction mistake or a supplier error, and to keep the printed value for disputes. Which schema design best supports this?

options.text: Extract `stated_total` and `calculated_total` plus a `conflict_detected` flag; code checks the arithmetic and routes conflicts.
options.why: Self-check fields make discrepancies explicit and verifiable.

options.text: Extract only `total` as printed, and have a downstream job recompute the line-item sum from the ERP's records.
options.why: This works partly, but the comparison happens late and without the extraction context.

options.text: Extract only `total`, and instruct the model to correct it when the line items don't add up, noting the correction.
options.why: This silently alters the financial record and loses the printed value.

options.text: Extract the line items only, and let the ERP compute every total itself, so model arithmetic is never trusted.
options.why: This loses the printed value needed for disputes and for detecting supplier errors.

questions.explanation: Design schemas with verification fields (`stated` vs `calculated`, conflict flags) that code can check.

questions.stem: Field accuracy is 98% on the five most common invoice layouts, but under 70% on rare ones: multi-page tables, totals printed at the top, and two-column layouts. The prompt currently includes three examples, all of common layouts. Which prompt improvement helps most?

options.text: Add 20 more examples of the common layouts, to reinforce the extraction pattern the model already handles well.
options.why: This reinforces what already works and costs tokens.

options.text: Add a paragraph explaining that layouts vary, and that totals and tables may appear in unexpected positions.
options.why: This describes the problem without showing how to handle it.

options.text: Route rare layouts automatically to human review, since they are only a small share of the weekly volume.
options.why: This gives up on an easily improved segment and adds reviewer load.

options.text: Replace some examples with ones covering rare structures (a multi-page table, a totals-first layout), with correct output.
options.why: Examples covering structural variety improve generalisation and reduce null or hallucinated extractions.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples should span the variety of document structures the system encounters.

questions.stem: The weekly backlog of 25,000 documents must be processed by Monday 09:00 for finance close. The team chooses overnight batch processing for the 50% cost saving. Which operating approach is sound?

options.text: Submit Monday at 06:00, since recent batches finished in under an hour, which leaves a comfortable two-hour margin.
options.why: Typical completion time isn't guaranteed. Batches have no latency SLA.

options.text: Submit early enough that a full 24-hour window still meets the deadline, track results by `custom_id`, and resubmit failures only.
options.why: Plan to the worst-case batch window rather than the typical latency, and retry selectively.

options.text: Run validation-retry loops inside each batch request with multi-turn tool calls, so every document is final when it returns.
options.why: Batch requests don't support multi-turn tool loops within a request.

options.text: Split the work into one batch per document type without request IDs, and match results back by their order.
options.why: Result order isn't a reliable key. Use `custom_id`.

questions.explanation: Batch SLA arithmetic: allow up to 24 hours, correlate by `custom_id`, and resubmit failures only.

questions.stem: A revised extraction prompt is ready. The team wants to run it on this week's full batch of 25,000 documents. What should they do first?

options.text: Run the full batch now, because it costs 50% less, then compare the results against last week's run.
options.why: A flawed prompt would waste the entire run, and fixing it means another full run.

options.text: Skip testing, since schema enforcement guarantees that the new output will be valid for the ERP.
options.why: Schemas don't guarantee semantic correctness.

options.text: Run a representative sample, measure accuracy by document type, fix problems, and then run the full batch.
options.why: Refining on a sample first avoids paying for a large flawed run.

options.text: Run the full batch synchronously instead, so problems surface immediately and the run can be stopped early.
options.why: This doubles the cost, and it is still the wrong order of operations.

questions.explanation: Iterate on a sample, then scale. This is a stated batch best practice.

questions.stem: A validation run shows 97% field-level accuracy overall, and leadership wants to auto-post every record to the ERP from next month. What is the main risk in that conclusion?

options.text: 97% is below the 99.5% industry standard for financial data, so the pipeline isn't ready for any automation yet.
options.why: Some segments may already be safe. The analysis needs to go down to the segment level.

options.text: The overall figure can hide weak segments (scanned customs forms, one language), so validate by document type and field first.
options.why: Aggregate metrics mask weak segments.

options.text: Field-level accuracy overstates quality. Only document-level accuracy (all fields correct) should be used for this decision.
options.why: Document-level metrics are useful too, but they still don't reveal which segments are weak.

options.text: There is no material risk, since 97% exceeds the accuracy of the manual entry clerks the pipeline replaces.
options.why: This ignores the variance across segments and the cost of errors in specific fields.

questions.explanation: Break accuracy down by document type and field before deciding what to automate.

questions.stem: Automation is live for invoices and bills of lading. Leadership asks how quality will be monitored over time, without reviewing every record, given that new suppliers and layouts keep appearing. What should the team do?

options.text: Audit only the records the model marked low confidence, since those are where errors are most likely to occur.
options.why: Confidently wrong records would never be audited.

options.text: Audit the first 200 records processed each Monday, which gives a consistent weekly sample at a fixed cost.
options.why: This sample isn't random, and it is biased toward particular suppliers and batches.

options.text: Stop auditing once three consecutive monthly audits show accuracy above target, then re-audit only after incidents.
options.why: Drift from new suppliers and layouts goes undetected.

options.text: Audit a stratified random sample of auto-posted records, across document types, suppliers and languages.
options.why: Stratified sampling detects drift in every segment, including rare ones.

questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling keeps quality visible across all segments.

questions.stem: The team wants per-field confidence scores to decide which records go to human review, instead of reviewing every customs form. Which TWO steps are required for this to work? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Calibrate the scores on a labelled validation set, so each threshold corresponds to a known error rate.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence can't be trusted for routing.

options.text: Route low-confidence fields, and records whose validations contradict each other, to human review.
options.why: This is the routing policy that calibration makes possible.

options.text: Use the model's raw self-reported confidence directly, since it already reflects uncertainty about each field.
options.why: Raw self-reports are poorly calibrated.

options.text: Apply one global threshold to every field and document type, so the routing rule is simple and easy to audit.
options.why: Calibration varies by field and segment, so a single untested threshold misroutes.

options.text: Send the high-confidence records to humans for spot-checking, since the low-confidence ones will be retried anyway.
options.why: That is backwards.

questions.explanation: Field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data, plus routing of low-confidence or contradictory items, makes human review efficient.

questions.stem: Customs packets of 80+ pages are processed in a single request. Fields printed on the first and last pages are extracted reliably, but fields in the middle pages are often missed. Which mitigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat the full list of fields at the end of the prompt, so the model is reminded of them after reading the packet.
options.why: This may help a little, but it doesn't fix weak attention over the middle pages.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens`, so the model has room to write out every field it finds in the packet.
options.why: That controls output length, not attention over the input.

options.text: Split the packet into logical sections, extract from each, then merge (or lead with a summary of key sections and headers).
options.why: This counters the lost-in-the-middle effect by restructuring the input.

options.text: Add an instruction asking the model to read every page carefully and not skip any section of the packet.
options.why: This is vague guidance that doesn't change how attention is distributed.

questions.explanation: Mitigate lost-in-the-middle by chunking, putting key information first and using section headers.

questions.stem: A bill of lading lists a gross weight of 12,400 kg on page 1 and 14,200 kg on page 3. The customs declaration depends on this figure. What should the extraction record?

options.text: The page-1 value, since header information on bills of lading is authoritative, with a note that page 3 differs.
options.why: This is an arbitrary rule, and the record is still treated as final.

options.text: Both values with their page numbers and a conflict flag, sending the record to review rather than picking one.
options.why: This preserves provenance and surfaces the conflict.

options.text: The higher value, since over-declaring weight is the safer error for customs and avoids penalties for under-declaring.
options.why: This is arbitrary and could itself be a legal misdeclaration.

options.text: The mean of the two values (13,300 kg), with a lowered confidence score, so the record can still be auto-posted.
options.why: That invents a value that neither page states.

questions.explanation: When sources conflict, keep both values with their provenance and flag the conflict.

questions.stem: The pipeline calls an MCP tool, `lookup_supplier(tax_id)`, to enrich records. It fails in three ways: the extracted tax ID is malformed, the supplier registry is temporarily down, or the caller lacks permission to see a restricted supplier. How should the tool respond?

options.text: Return `null` in all three cases, and let the pipeline treat a missing supplier the same way however it arose.
options.why: The pipeline can't decide how to recover if every failure looks the same.

options.text: Retry inside the tool with exponential backoff until it succeeds, so callers always receive a supplier record.
options.why: Validation and permission errors never succeed on retry.

options.text: Return a placeholder supplier marked "pending enrichment", so the record posts and is corrected later.
options.why: This corrupts ERP data with placeholder records.

options.text: Return `isError: true` with a category per case (validation, transient and retryable, permission) and a clear message.
options.why: Distinct categories let the pipeline retry, fix the input or escalate as appropriate.

questions.explanation: Structured MCP error categories (transient, validation, business, permission) drive the correct recovery strategy.
